Why I made Cinnamon my default Desktop

Isn't it nice to run a desktop environment on a desktop? LOL That was the first thing that I did not like when I "upgraded" from Win 7 to 8. I was so happy to see Cinnamon when I moved to Mint a couple of years ago. I'm glad that it can be used with Ubuntu. I have heard some complaints about Unity trying to be everything like Win 8 did.

I am new to Linux. Installed in many times and then threw it away because it was not user friendly.

But a month ago I installed Mint with this Cinnamon, and instantly liked it. It is this that pushed me to use Linux, and it is this that make me feel that this is a valid Windows replacement.

And as far as I have learned about Linux Mint now, is appears to be based on older code. Code that matured. And from simple user point of view, that is what I need. Not the shiny flashy new things but something that I know that will be there when I reboot the machine. Something that looks familiar.
Anything is better compared to Unity. Mate and Cinnamon are all I've been using for the past year since I dropped gnome.

You've made me decide to try out Cinnamon.

I actually like Unity because it saves precious vertical screen space by merging the desktop top bar, the window's title bar and the window's menu bar into one. It works quite well. I have no use for the launcher bar but I can auto‐hide it. The Super key will show it if I need it. It also reveals the top bar and clock even when I have something in full screen mode. I have no use for the whole “lenses” feature they apparently spend a lot of resources developing, but I can set the launcher to do only the one thing I do like: partial text searching to launch applications.

Unity still has some disadvantages though.

We had to wait a while for the option to keep menu bars on the windows when they were not maximized. It's still not the default. Of all the things to copy from MacOS, they copy the most confusing legacy design feature.

They came up with a creative way to try to show scroll bars only when you need them. It was worth trying, but I found it hard to use. You can switch back to regular scroll bars with a third‐party settings manager, but the scroll bars are sometimes unresponsive. I think this is because under the hood it's still waiting for the trigger to show the scrollbar before it responds to your mouse.

While Unity is open source and problems under the hood can be detected, Canonical intentionally introduced a security hole by sending users' keyboard input to Amazon. The problem wasn't that they were trying to make money displaying Amazon ads in the Unity dash search results. It was that they didn't immediately realize how big of a security hole this was and it took them about 2 years to take it out. Unity will finally stop sending your search strings to Amazon in the upcoming LTS release. Until then, we will continue disabling the feature ourselves.

Unity is the only desktop environment that will be using Canonical's own Wayland compositor. Everything else is going to adopt the community's Mir compositor. That leaves Canonical on their own to support one of the most complicated and legacy feature loaded parts of a desktop system. I'm expecting incompatibilities and long standing bugs.

Finally, Unity is pretty bad with resource consumption for what it provides. I'm not sure if that will ever improve. Either they don't bother programming efficiency, or they're doing a lot of useless stuff in the background that I don't need. It also has stability problems.

I don't think Cinnamon does the nice features quite as well—merging all three horizontal bars really is perfect in Unity—but it seems to do a half decent job and it lacks all of the problems I mentioned. If it's noticeably lighter and faster than Unity I'll probably switch to it.

BTW, the desktop switching works about as well in Unity. You have to open the settings to add more, but it puts them in a grid instead of a long list for faster switching.
